title: FMGE PSM Day 1 Mock
subject: Community Medicine
description: A 41-question PSM mock from the reviewed Day 1 notes.

questions.stem: A 10-year exposure cohort loses many participants before outcome assessment. Which problem is most characteristic?
questions.explanation: A long cohort can be distorted when participants disappear before outcome assessment; this is loss to follow-up. Recall bias is not the characteristic limitation emphasized for this design.

questions.stem: Who is credited with the standard definition of epidemiology?
questions.explanation: John M Last is credited with the standard definition of epidemiology used in this material.

questions.stem: A researcher wants to study possible risk factors for a very rare cancer. Which of the following designs is most efficient?
questions.explanation: Case-control studies are efficient for rare diseases, whereas a cohort design is comparatively unsuitable for that purpose.

questions.stem: Investigators assign no exposure and compare naturally exposed and unexposed groups specifically to test an exposure-disease hypothesis. How should the study be classified?
questions.explanation: Testing an exposure-disease hypothesis places the study in the analytical category rather than the descriptive category.

questions.stem: Which three dimensions describe disease distribution in epidemiology?
questions.explanation: Disease distribution is classically described in terms of time, place and person.

questions.stem: District-level fluoride exposure is correlated with district-level fluorosis rates. What is the unit of analysis?
questions.explanation: The population or group is the unit of analysis in an ecological study; measurements are aggregated across its members.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the principal vector of Japanese encephalitis?
questions.explanation: Japanese encephalitis is transmitted by Culex tritaeniorhynchus rather than Aedes aegypti.

questions.stem: Factory workers improve hand-hygiene only because they know they are being observed. Which bias is illustrated?
questions.explanation: The Hawthorne effect is behavioral change because subjects know they are being observed; recall bias instead concerns remembering past exposure.

questions.stem: Duffy-negative individuals are relatively protected against which malaria species?
questions.explanation: Duffy-negative phenotype reduces susceptibility to Plasmodium vivax malaria, but protection is not absolute; infections in Duffy-negative people have been documented.

questions.stem: Interviewer bias is most likely when:
options: Outcome is assessed with the same protocol in all participants
Participants with disease remember past exposure differently
Cases and controls are questioned with different intensity
Exposure is recorded before disease develops
questions.explanation: Interviewer bias results when the interviewer probes comparison groups differently. Unequal remembering by participants is a different error mechanism.
questions.answer_label: Cases and controls are questioned with different intensity
questions.answer: Cases and controls are questioned with different intensity

questions.stem: Disease-free exposed and unexposed groups are followed forward until outcomes occur. Which of the following measures of association is directly appropriate?
questions.source: PDF p.19, p.20, p.28 | E2 | Multi-page
questions.explanation: Following exposed and unexposed groups forward permits direct comparison of their risks; the resulting ratio is relative risk.

questions.stem: What age range defines adolescence?
questions.explanation: Adolescence spans 10-19 years.

questions.stem: Berksonian bias most directly results from:
options: Different rates of hospital admission among comparison groups
questions.explanation: Berksonian bias arises when hospital admission rates differ among comparison groups.
questions.answer_label: Different rates of hospital admission among comparison groups
questions.answer: Different rates of hospital admission among comparison groups

questions.stem: Which of the following broad study categories includes a field trial?
questions.explanation: Field trials belong to the experimental/interventional class of epidemiological studies.

questions.stem: Participants and investigators are unaware of treatment allocation, but the data analyst is aware. What is this blinding design?
questions.explanation: Double blinding keeps both subjects and investigators unaware; triple blinding additionally includes the analyzer.

questions.stem: What does the Pygmalion effect describe?
options: Improved performance due to higher expectations
Distorted recall of a past exposure
Change in laboratory measurement over time
questions.explanation: The Pygmalion effect describes improved performance produced by higher expectations from another person, such as a teacher.
questions.answer_label: Improved performance due to higher expectations
questions.answer: Improved performance due to higher expectations

questions.stem: Investigators deliberately assign patients with higher fever to the experimental arm. Which design step, used with allocation concealment, reduces this selection bias?
questions.explanation: Randomization with concealed allocation prevents investigators from choosing the treatment arm for each patient and balances baseline characteristics in expectation. Chance imbalances can still occur, especially in small trials.

questions.stem: Among cases, 60 were exposed and 20 unexposed; among controls, 30 were exposed and 60 unexposed. What are the odds ratio and interpretation?
questions.explanation: The odds ratio is \((60 \times 60)/(20 \times 30)=6\). Because it is greater than 1, the association is positive.

questions.stem: What is the comparison arm called in a controlled therapeutic trial?
questions.explanation: A controlled therapeutic trial compares the experimental group with a reference group.

questions.stem: First-in-human testing of a new drug in healthy volunteers primarily assesses what?
questions.explanation: First-in-human work in healthy volunteers focuses primarily on safety and non-toxicity/tolerability rather than therapeutic efficacy.

questions.stem: Who proposed the germ theory of disease?
questions.explanation: The germ theory of disease is attributed to Louis Pasteur.

questions.stem: A marketed drug is being monitored for uncommon and long-term adverse effects. Which phase does this represent?
questions.explanation: Post-marketing surveillance after launch is Phase IV and is used to identify uncommon or long-term adverse effects.

questions.stem: What are the three components of the epidemiological triad?
questions.explanation: The epidemiological triad consists of agent, host and environment.

questions.stem: A chronic disease has several interconnected determinants and multiple possible intervention points. Which causation model best represents this?
questions.explanation: A network of interacting determinants with several possible intervention points is represented by the web of causation.

questions.stem: In a study of physical inactivity and hypertension, age is related to both exposure and outcome. Investigators want equal age distributions between comparison groups before analysis. Which method should be used?
questions.explanation: Age is acting as a confounder because it is related to both exposure and outcome. Matching equalizes its distribution between comparison groups.

questions.stem: What is the natural history of disease?
options: Frequency of disease in a population
questions.explanation: Natural history is the progression of disease in the body without intervention.

questions.stem: Pathological changes are present, but symptoms have not yet begun. Which stage of disease is this?
questions.explanation: Pathological changes before the onset of symptoms correspond to the subclinical stage.

questions.stem: Where is WHO headquarters located?
questions.explanation: WHO headquarters is in Geneva.

questions.stem: During one year, 40 new cases occur among 2,000 disease-free people at risk. What is the incidence per 1,000?
questions.explanation: Incidence counts new cases among the population at risk. \(40/2000 \times 1000 = 20\) per 1,000.

questions.stem: Where is UNICEF headquarters located?
questions.explanation: UNICEF headquarters is in New York.

questions.stem: All of the following are principal bodies of WHO EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: WHO's principal bodies include the World Health Assembly, Executive Board and Secretariat; General Conference is not one of them.

questions.stem: The epidemiologist associated with this map also compared cholera mortality among households supplied by different water companies without assigning their water source. Which study design was this?
questions.image_alt: Street map with cholera deaths and water-pump locations
questions.image_source: p.57 | left street map of cholera deaths and water pumps; crop the map only and exclude the handwritten “SPOT MAP” label
questions.source: PDF p.56, p.57, p.58 | E2 | Multi-page/Diagram
questions.explanation: The map identifies John Snow’s Broad Street cholera investigation. His separate comparison of households served by different water companies was a natural experiment: water source varied without researcher allocation. The spot map itself is descriptive.

questions.stem: How many Sustainable Development Goals are there?
questions.explanation: The Sustainable Development Goal framework contains 17 goals.

questions.stem: All of the following are components of GOBI-FFF EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: GOBI-FFF includes oral rehydration, breastfeeding and family planning; vitamin A supplementation is not one of the acronym's components.

questions.stem: Which Sustainable Development Goal is titled Good Health and Well-being?
questions.explanation: Good Health and Well-being is Sustainable Development Goal 3.

questions.stem: The global maternal mortality ratio falls to 68 per 100,000 live births. Does this meet the numerical threshold in SDG target 3.1?
options: No, it remains above the target
Yes, it is within the target
No, it is exactly at the target
It cannot be assessed from the value
questions.explanation: SDG target 3.1 calls for a global maternal mortality ratio below 70 per 100,000 live births by 2030. A global value of 68 meets that numerical threshold.
questions.answer_label: Yes, it is within the target
questions.answer: Yes, it is within the target

questions.stem: Which of the following is a Category B bioterrorism agent?
questions.explanation: Ricin toxin is a Category B bioterrorism agent.

questions.stem: A surveillance officer must identify an event belonging to the fixed always-notifiable group under IHR. Which of the following qualifies?
questions.explanation: SARS belongs to the fixed group of conditions requiring notification under the International Health Regulations.

questions.stem: Under WHO’s January 2021 guidance, a laboratory moves from non-propagative SARS-CoV-2 diagnostic testing to viral culture and isolation. Which biosafety change was recommended?
questions.explanation: WHO’s January 2021 guidance recommended BSL-2-equivalent controls for non-propagative diagnostic work and BSL-3 controls for virus culture. The 2024 update allows less stringent controls for some currently circulating strains following a local risk assessment, so this historical distinction is not a universal current requirement.

questions.stem: Which of the following best defines emporiatrics?
questions.explanation: Emporiatrics concerns the health of international travellers.

questions.stem: A chronic disease has incidence 2 per 1,000 per year and average duration 4 years. What is the approximate prevalence per 1,000?
questions.explanation: Prevalence is approximately incidence multiplied by duration. \(2 \times 4 = 8\) per 1,000.
